headline.text: The FDA label describes potentially additive central nervous system effects with efavirenz and alcohol.

reported.text: The controlled study found unchanged intoxication and drowsiness despite lower blood alcohol concentrations after efavirenz-containing therapy.
Alcohol did not alter efavirenz pharmacokinetics in that study.

claims.text: The FDA label describes potentially additive central nervous system effects when efavirenz is combined with alcohol.
claims.quote: Patients receiving efavirenz should be alerted to the potential for additive central nervous system effects when efavirenz is used concomitantly with alcohol or psychoactive drugs.
claims.judgeRationale: The label warns of potential additive CNS effects when efavirenz is used with alcohol.

claims.text: A controlled study found unchanged intoxication and drowsiness ratings after efavirenz-containing therapy despite lower blood alcohol concentrations, suggesting a pharmacodynamic interaction.
claims.quote: A pharmacodynamic interaction between alcohol and efavirenz was observed as evidenced by no change in intoxication or drowsiness before and after efavirenz ART despite lower BAC.
claims.judgeRationale: The randomized placebo-controlled study reports unchanged intoxication and drowsiness after efavirenz therapy despite lower BAC and calls this a pharmacodynamic interaction.

claims.text: The study found that alcohol did not alter efavirenz pharmacokinetics.
claims.quote: No effect of alcohol on ritonavir or efavirenz pharmacokinetics was observed.
claims.judgeRationale: The abstract states that alcohol had no effect on efavirenz pharmacokinetics.
